title: New Orleans musicians versus young players today
summary: He says New Orleans men had better training than today's riff players, and notes young Black musicians now entering symphonies.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah, I was going to say, maybe we could interview him too while I'm trying to get on the story, but you know, I didn't know he was dead. Well, what kind of music did the Chicago musicians play? I'm not trying to ask you to run down the music or anything of that kind. I mean, the New Orleans type, you know, was quite different, but I mean, did it compare? Is it good dance music or is it a different type or?
Well, it's, that is, if you want to compare it in the Dixieland field, then it is different. It is different.

I was just trying to put you on the spot because I know you have friends from New Orleans and friends here too. But I don't mind that. Of course, in those days, most of those people aren't playing anymore anyway. I wondered if you could compare what types of musicians here.

Because they don't match up. They don't match up with those boys. They don't match up with those boys. And I'm not afraid to say it because they have not developed themselves musically. See, you take the young fella today after he's had a few lessons and he can run a few scales and he play a few, what they call riffs, then he stops right there. See? And he gets in what they call a combo and that's as far as he goes. Half of the time you hear him play, you don't know what he's playing.
And of course, people are accepting it and they tell you, well, it pays, yes, it pays, but where are you getting?
The New Orleans fellas, you felt, had higher musicianship, higher quality training.

Oh, I'm not afraid to say that, by all means. Do you think they're in college? Oh, there are, and there are a number, of course. Now there is an evolution that's taking place now that I'm very happy over. That among the younger fellas who are in college now, you'd be surprised at the number of young people who are going in for the serious side of music. And they are meeting with great success and now that the field is broadening and that this prejudice is dying out, there are many, many openings that they are getting into now that are here to fall. They didn't get a chance to enjoy. Now we have one man who's going in, one of our boys, who's going in Grand Park Symphony next month. What instrument? What instrument? He's, oh, Shello. Shello. A man by the name of Donald White. He is now with the Cleveland Symphony, has been with the Cleveland Symphony this his second year. We have another chap from Chicago here, bass, violinist, Richard Davis. He took the audition for the St. Louis Symphony. He was offered the chair, but he refused it because he's with Sarah Vaughan, where he makes triple the salary that the symphony pays. But the opening is there for him anytime that he wants it. What is his name again? Richard Davis. Richard Davis. Mm-hmm. He's in, he's in Sweden now with Sarah Vaughan. I had a card for him the other day.
